## Data sources and updates

The site combines three data streams: PRISM gridded temperature and precipitation, RCC-ACIS station observations, and SNODAS modeled snowpack. Their reporting dates, reference periods, and quality checks differ; use the date and legend shown on each map or explorer rather than assuming all products describe the same day.

### PRISM temperature and precipitation

These maps use daily, approximately 4-km precipitation and maximum- and minimum-temperature grids produced by the [PRISM Climate Group at Oregon State University](https://prism.oregonstate.edu/data/). We retrieve the PRISM grids through the [RCC-ACIS web service](https://www.rcc-acis.org/docs_webservices.html) for Arizona, New Mexico, and a half-degree buffer around the two states. Temperature is shown in °F and precipitation in inches. Mean temperature is calculated at each grid cell as the average of that day's maximum and minimum. PRISM grids are spatial estimates informed by weather-station data, not direct observations at every pixel.

**Recent maps mostly use preliminary data.** According to [PRISM's update calendar](https://prism.oregonstate.edu/calendar/), a day's first grid is modeled about 24 hours after the day ends, then modeled again after about five days and roughly monthly through six months. The eighth daily run is considered final unless the whole dataset is later revised. Our daily update checks for newly available dates *and* revisits recent dates so revised PRISM values can flow into the maps. The date printed on each map is the latest PRISM date actually used; it may lag today's date. Recent values and derived rankings can change as their source grids are revised. These maps do not use the separate PRISM monthly dataset.

## Reference periods and interpretation

Unless a PRISM map says otherwise, its comparison period is **1991–2020**. For a daily seasonal comparison, we combine the same calendar date and the two days on either side in each of those 30 years (about 150 values per grid cell). For a 7-, 30-, 90-, or 180-day map, we compare the *whole period's* result with historical periods ending in that centered five-day calendar window. A percentile rank describes position within that historical distribution: low ranks are relatively low values, high ranks relatively high values. Thus, a high temperature rank means unusual warmth, while a high dry-spell rank means an unusually *long* dry spell. Labels such as **exceptionally low** and **exceptionally high** refer to this comparison sample, not an all-time record. The legend on each map gives its exact ranges and units. Station ranks and snow comparisons use the different reference periods described below.

The PRISM maps below use a **wet-day threshold of at least 0.04 inch**, a **freeze threshold of minimum temperature at or below 32°F**, and a **water year of October 1–September 30**. Blank areas can mean that an event did not occur or that the available comparison is unreliable; see the relevant method below. The snow mapping season is October–May, not a full water year.

## Temperature maps

- **Current values:** Show the latest day's maximum, minimum, or derived mean temperature. These are absolute temperatures, not departures from normal.
- **Daily departures:** Subtract the matching 1991–2020 calendar-day mean from the latest maximum, minimum, or mean temperature. Positive values are warmer than average; negative values are cooler.
- **30-day departures:** Average the latest 30 daily temperatures and subtract the average of their matching daily normals. This highlights sustained warmth or coolness rather than one-day swings.
- **Daily percentile ranks:** Rank the latest maximum, minimum, or mean temperature against the centered five-day historical sample. High ranks mean unusual warmth for the date; low ranks mean unusual coolness.
- **7-, 30-, and 90-day mean-temperature ranks:** First average daily mean temperature over the complete period, then rank that period average against seasonally matched historical period averages. These are *not* averages of daily ranks.
- **Extreme warm days and cold nights:** Count, over the latest 30 days, maximum temperatures strictly above the local daily 90th-percentile threshold and minimum temperatures strictly below the local daily 10th-percentile threshold, respectively.
- **Freeze-night count and anomaly:** Count nights at or below 32°F in the latest 30 days. The anomaly subtracts the average count for seasonally matched 1991–2020 periods; positive values mean more freeze nights than usual.
- **First- and last-freeze date and departure:** Find the first or last night at or below 32°F in an August 1–July 31 cold season. Departure compares the observed date with the local 1991–2020 median; negative means earlier, positive later. Current-season dates may change, and areas without a freeze or a reliable historical comparison are blank.
- **Freeze-free season length and departure:** Count days from the last January–July freeze to the first August–December freeze in the same calendar year. Departure is relative to the 1991–2020 median length. Areas missing either event are blank; an in-progress season is provisional.

## Precipitation maps

- **Recent totals:** Sum daily precipitation for the latest complete day or latest 7, 30, or 90 days. These maps show amounts, not how unusual the amounts are.
- **7-, 30-, and 90-day percentile ranks:** Rank each accumulation against seasonally matched 1991–2020 accumulations. Low ranks indicate unusually dry periods; high ranks indicate unusually wet ones.
- **30- and 90-day percent of normal:** Divide the recent total by the matching 1991–2020 average and multiply by 100. Below 100% is drier than average; above 100% is wetter. Areas with a historical average below 0.10 inch are blank because the ratio would be unstable.
- **Recent change in 30-day rank:** Subtract the 30-day precipitation rank from 14 days ago from the latest 30-day rank. Positive values indicate relative wetting and negative values relative drying; the units are percentile points, not inches.
- **Current dry spell:** Count consecutive days below 0.04 inch ending on the latest day, and rank that length against seasonally matched historical spells. Zero means the latest day was wet; a high rank means an unusually long ongoing dry spell.
- **Longest dry spell in 180 days:** Find the longest below-threshold run anywhere in the latest 180 days, whether or not it is still underway. Its companion rank compares that maximum with seasonally matched 1991–2020 windows.
- **Wet-day count in 90 days:** Count days with at least 0.04 inch. Its companion rank shows whether wet days have been unusually frequent or scarce for the season; it does not measure the size of those events.
- **Mean precipitation per wet day:** Average precipitation on qualifying wet days in the latest 90 days. Its companion rank compares that intensity with seasonally matched historical periods. Areas with no wet days are blank.
- **Very-wet-day contribution:** Calculate the share of the latest 90-day total supplied by days above the local 1991–2020 annual wet-day 95th-percentile amount. Its companion rank shows whether that share is unusual for the season. Totals below 0.10 inch are blank.
- **Water-year total, percent of normal, and rank:** Accumulate precipitation since October 1. Percent of normal compares with the 1991–2020 average through the *same date*; the rank compares with historical water-year-to-date totals through that date. A low rank means an unusually dry water year so far.
- **Water-year maximum three-day precipitation and rank:** Find the largest complete three-day total since October 1. These maps wait for data through October 3 rather than treating one or two days as a three-day event. The rank compares with annual maxima from complete 1991–2020 water years, so the current year's result remains provisional until September 30.
- **Water-year precipitation concentration:** Divide the largest three-day total by the water-year total. High percentages mean that one short period supplied a larger share of the year's precipitation. Totals below 0.10 inch are blank.

## Daily Explorer

- **Daily maps:** Show precipitation and maximum, minimum, and derived mean temperature from the same cached PRISM daily grids used elsewhere on the site. Mean temperature requires both maximum and minimum at that cell; missing inputs are not filled. Temperature can be viewed as an absolute value or departure from its 1991–2020 centered-five-day calendar-day mean. Fixed color classes make days comparable. Source reporting dates do not necessarily represent a local midnight-to-midnight observing day.
- **Regional summaries:** Use native grid cells whose centers fall within Arizona or New Mexico, weighted by cell area. The combined region is area-weighted, not a simple average of the two state means. Each statistic requires usable data over at least 95% of its region; paired reference data are also required for departures and threshold comparisons. Missing values are unavailable, not zero. Changing the summary region changes statistics and rankings, not the map footprint.
- **Finding wet days:** Metrics include regional mean precipitation, the area receiving at least 0.10, 0.50, or 1 inch, and the spatial 99th-percentile amount. That last metric describes the distribution across the region on that day, including dry cells; it is **not a historical percentile**.
- **Finding warm, cold, and freezing days:** Metrics include regional temperature and departure, the area above the local daily 90th percentile or below the 10th percentile for maximum or minimum temperature, and the area with minimum temperature at or below 32°F. Thresholds use the 1991–2020 centered-five-day reference. Mean-temperature percentile coverage is not calculated. These measures help find unusual patterns; they are not verified impacts or formal annual extremes indices.
- **Timeline and map grids:** Single-day view shows the selected season's timeline. The seven-day grid is centered on the selected date; the 30-day grid ends on that date, and the timeline follows the grid's date range. Available built dates can cross season and water-year boundaries; unavailable dates remain gaps. Notable days are ordered within the selected season and region, not ranked against the historical record.
- **Available dates and updates:** The published collection grows through the current water year and retains the preceding September for early-October comparisons. It only includes dates with cached inputs; it is not yet an all-years daily archive. Revised inputs trigger rebuilding of affected dates; unchanged maps are reused.
- **Forecast discussion context:** The selected-day discussion panel links to NWS office AFDs and WPC-issued text archived by Iowa Environmental Mesonet (IEM). Searches cover issuances during that UTC date, oldest first, up to 100 results—not necessarily forecasts valid for that day. Multiple issuances, updates and corrections may be present; archive gaps or non-issued event products can produce empty results. National discussions are not filtered to the map region. Read issue and valid times in the original text: PRISM reporting days may differ from UTC days, and forecast reasoning is not a verified account of observed outcomes. Selecting a product loads IEM's response directly into a scrollable reader; a new-tab fallback remains available. No text is downloaded during daily publishing, summarized or certified by this site. Changing the selected date clears the reader.

## Weather maps

- **Source and timing:** When available in Daily Explorer, circulation maps use [NOAA CPC CORe](https://www.cpc.ncep.noaa.gov/products/CORe/index.html) reanalysis ensemble means. Daily fields average eight samples at 00, 03, …, 21 UTC. These are modeled atmospheric analyses, not forecasts or direct observations, and their UTC dates need not match PRISM daily reporting periods exactly.
- **500-mb heights:** Geopotential height is shown in decameters (dam), with contours every 6 dam. Thicker 30-dam index contours and modest emphasis on 588/594 dam help follow patterns; they are visual references, not thresholds for unusual heat or an exceptionally strong ridge. All dates use the same 480–612 dam color scale. Shading shows absolute heights, not anomalies.
- **250-mb jet:** Shading is the speed calculated from the daily-mean eastward and northward wind components, converted to knots. It is not mean instantaneous speed, the day's maximum wind, or a surface gust. Streamlines depict the mean flow, not storm tracks or air-parcel trajectories. Purple outlines locate Arizona and New Mexico within the Pacific–North American context.
- **Moisture and low-level flow:** Total-column precipitable water is shown in inches on a fixed 0–3+ scale; values above 3 inches share the darkest color without altering the underlying data. Sea-level pressure contours are spaced every 4 hPa. Arrows show daily-mean 850-mb winds, omitted wherever that level is below terrain or surface pressure is unavailable at any of the eight daily samples. These winds are not integrated vapor transport or surface winds. Blue H/red L labels identify filtered daily-mean pressure centers with central pressure in hPa; they are not tracked storms. Sea-level pressure over elevated terrain requires caution, and elevated-terrain center candidates are screened using the complete daily-mean surface pressure. If hourly terrain-screening inputs are missing, PWAT, pressure contours and independently screened H/L labels remain available while winds are withheld, with a notice on the map.
- **Availability and retention:** Weather maps follow the exact selected date; a missing date is shown as unavailable rather than replaced with another day. Recent inputs are rechecked within a bounded three-day window; revisions can rebuild affected maps, while verified unchanged maps are reused. The weather collection grows and retains built dates, with older Explorer dates filled in resumable batches. Historical reanalysis may also be revised outside that short recheck window. Weather outages do not prevent core PRISM, snow and station publication. A single circulation pattern does not establish ENSO attribution; no weather-map anomaly baseline is included yet.

## Station Conditions

- **Source and network:** Station observations come from RCC-ACIS, separately from the PRISM grids. The network combines long-record stations and ThreadEx area series with surrounding regional stations. ThreadEx records can join observations from different sites over time: they appear in the tables but are not plotted as single physical station locations. Station history, record length, reporting time, and completeness vary; these records are not necessarily homogeneous climate series.
- **Summary periods:** Precipitation is summed and mean temperature averages daily `(maximum + minimum) / 2` pairs over 7, 30, or 90 days, or rolling 6- or 12-calendar-month periods. Calendar-month periods have variable day counts. The map, popups, and tables use the displayed start and end dates together.
- **Precipitation completeness:** Departures, ranks, and percentiles require a complete period. An observed total may be shown as a provisional lower bound (`≥`, dashed map outline) if only the latest one or two reports are missing, with at most one missing for a seven-day period. Its comparisons are withheld. Interior gaps, larger lags, quality flags, or an outdated cache make the value unavailable. Trace precipitation counts as zero; accumulated reports that cannot be assigned to individual days are excluded.
- **Temperature completeness:** Means require at least 95% of paired daily observations, no gap longer than two days, and no quality-flagged observations. Coverage of 95–<98% carries an asterisk and dashed outline; at least 98% displays normally. Historical temperature comparisons use the same completeness rules. No missing temperatures are estimated.
- **Departures:** Subtract the average of eligible matching-period values from **1991–2020**. At least 15 comparison years are required; 15–19 carry a limited-sample caution. Precipitation compares totals, while temperature compares means.
- **Percentiles, ranks, and comparable highs:** Use one eligible period ending on the same calendar date in each earlier usable year of that station's record, excluding the current year. At least 25 years are required; 25–29 carry a limited-sample caution. The percentile is `100 × (number lower + 0.5 × number tied) / n`; rank 1 is wettest or warmest. February 29 comparisons use leap years only. Each station's comparison years and sample count are shown. The popup's highest comparable period uses those same calendar-matched windows, plus the current period if it sets or ties the high; the date is the window's ending date, with the latest tie shown. It is not the maximum over every possible rolling window in the record.
- **Recent extremes and persistence:** Show the wettest day, wettest three consecutive days, highest maximum, lowest minimum, unusually hot days, unusually warm nights, longest unusually hot run, and longest dry run in the selected period. Hot days and warm nights exceed the respective centered-five-day 1991–2020 90th-percentile threshold; dry days have less than 0.04 inch. Extremes require complete, unflagged observations for the relevant variable; temperature-threshold indicators require at least 15 baseline years for every day. These are selected-period indicators, not formal annual/monthly Climdex products or all-time records. Daily charts identify the dates and values of the four amount/temperature extremes; a three-day total spans three bars rather than being assigned to one day.
- **Cool-season freeze nights:** Count minimum temperatures at or below 32°F from October 1 through March 31, season-to-date through March; April–September retains the completed season. This count does not change with the rolling-period selector. Departure subtracts the average count through the matching seasonal date in at least 15 complete 1991–2020 seasons. Positive means more freeze nights than average. Incomplete current counts or insufficient historical comparisons are withheld, not filled with nonfreezing nights.
- **Updates and cautions:** Daily histories are cached between runs and recent reports are rechecked for late arrivals or revisions. The page shows its verified snapshot date; lagging or unavailable stations are not silently carried forward. Map outlines, symbols, popup explanations, table notes, and coverage reports distinguish partial values, limited reference samples, and unavailable comparisons. Basemap tiles provide geographic context, not climate data.

## Snow maps (SNODAS)

Snow maps use daily modeled SWE and snow-depth grids from the [NOAA/NSIDC SNODAS masked archive](https://noaadata.apps.nsidc.org/NOAA/G02158/masked/). SWE is the liquid-water equivalent stored in the snowpack, expressed here in inches; it is **not snow depth or daily snowfall**. Maps represent the source's 06:00 UTC snapshot. Regional grids are aligned by nearest-neighbor sampling to a fixed common grid so the earlier and later source-grid layouts can be compared without smoothing their values.

- **Season and updates:** Current Snow covers October 1–May 31 and uses the latest verified daily pair, which can lag PRISM and station dates. Updates run during that season, with a June 1–14 closeout for late May data. A snow season is labeled by the year in which May falls; WY2027 snow maps therefore cover October 2026–May 2027, not the entire October–September water year.
- **Daily reference:** Uses **WY2005–WY2025**, an internal 21-season SNODAS reference, not a 30-year climate normal. For each calendar date, take each year's median SWE within the centered five-day window, requiring at least three valid days, then take the median across eligible years. Each year receives equal weight. At October and May season edges, only in-season days are used. The cached daily median requires at least 15 eligible years per cell.
- **Observed SWE:** Shows screened modeled snowpack water on the map date. Valid zero values indicate no modeled snow water; missing or rejected cells are not treated as zero.
- **Departure from median:** Observed SWE minus the date-specific reference median, in inches. Positive means more snow water than typical for that date. This is an absolute difference, not a percentile or a departure from the seasonal maximum.
- **Percent of median:** Observed SWE divided by the same date-specific median, times 100. This map requires at least **18 reference years** and a median of at least **1 inch** to avoid unstable ratios over typically snow-free areas. A valid zero observation can be 0%; 100% equals the median and 200% is twice it. Gray means a supported median below 1 inch, while beige means missing data or insufficient reference support. The ≥200% category is open-ended; values are not capped. This is **not a percentile**.
- **Seven-day net SWE change:** Subtract SWE on exactly date D−7 from SWE on date D, in inches. Positive means net snowpack-water gain; negative means net loss. This is neither snowfall nor melt alone. Both exact endpoints must be verified and pass quality checks; the intervening six dates are not required. A missing or quality-held prior endpoint produces a dated unavailable notice instead of substituting another date or retaining an older change map.
- **Quality safeguards:** SWE/depth pairs are screened for one-sided missing data, SWE exceeding depth, and invalid ranges; source files are unchanged. Current maps require at least 80% valid regional coverage and reference overlap over at least 80% of valid observed cells. Paired-QC exclusions or observed/reference SWE at or above 50 inches trigger a publication hold, not an automatic physical cap. The prior change endpoint must pass the corresponding daily-data checks, and the change requires at least 80% shared valid regional coverage. A hold retains the last approved current maps; when no approved map exists for the new season, the page shows a waiting notice. Map dates identify the data actually displayed.

## Historic Years

Each available Historic Years page summarizes a water year without labeling the year itself as an El Niño or La Niña event. A separate badge reports the December–February [Relative Oceanic Niño Index (RONI)](https://www.cpc.ncep.noaa.gov/products/analysis_monitoring/enso/roni/) value and its phase for that three-month period; it does not establish the cause of Southwest conditions.

- **October–March cool season:** Maps show precipitation total and rank, maximum- and minimum-temperature departures, wet-day-count rank, and mean precipitation per wet day. The temperature departures use 1991–2020 daily normals.
- **Full water year:** Maps show October–September precipitation total and rank. Cool-season and full-year precipitation ranks, plus cool-season wet-day-count ranks, use a fixed set of complete water years **1982–2025** (44 seasons), including the displayed year. These full-season ranks have fewer reference values than the current, seasonally matched rolling maps.
- **Completed snow season:** Where SNODAS is available, peak SWE is the maximum screened daily SWE during October–May, and snow-covered days count valid days with SWE of at least **0.1 inch**. Each cell needs valid observations on at least **90% of all calendar days** in that season, including source-missing dates; otherwise both values are withheld. Snow-day counts are not expanded to fill gaps, and peak values can miss events on unavailable days. Documented suspect peak cells are masked separately from the unchanged source grids. These maps describe peak water storage and snow persistence, not accumulated snowfall. Seasonal peak-SWE anomaly and percent-of-median products remain development pilots and are not yet part of Historic Years.

The data-processing and map-generation methods are available in the [Southwest Climate Watch GitHub repository](https://github.com/mcrimmins/SWClimateWatch).
